Greek letters, in alphabet order.Alpha: Together with beta it gives us the word alphabet; the letter descends from the Phoenician aleph, meaning ox, and the shape began as an ox head.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Gamma: Ernest Rutherford named gamma rays after this third letter around 1903; they are the most energetic form of electromagnetic radiation.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Epsilon: Mathematicians use epsilon for an arbitrarily tiny quantity, so much that a tiny positive number is jokingly called an epsilon.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Eta: Capital eta looks like an English H because it began as an h sound before becoming a long e; in physics and engineering it often stands for efficiency.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Theta: The circle with a bar is the standard symbol for an angle in trigonometry, and in neuroscience it names a slow brainwave rhythm.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Lambda: Spartan warriors painted this letter on their shields as the emblem of Lacedaemon, and physicists use it as the symbol for wavelength.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Pi: As a letter it is only the Greek p, but William Jones first used it for the circle constant in 1706 and Euler's use made it standard.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Sigma: Capital sigma means sum in mathematics, and the lowercase letter has a special final form, written like a small s with a tail, used only at word ends.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Phi: The golden ratio, about 1.618, is called phi, reportedly in honour of the Greek sculptor Phidias, whose works were said to use it.
Greek letters, in alphabet order.Omega: Its name means big o, set against omicron, little o; 'the alpha and the omega' in the Bible means the beginning and the end.

Europe's earthquakes, in order.Basel, Switzerland: Basel was hit by what's considered Central Europe's strongest historical quake, and the earthquake and fires destroyed much of the city.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Lisbon, Portugal: The Lisbon quake struck on All Saints' Day, and it was followed by a tsunami and fire, shaking the optimism of Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Calabria, Italy: The Calabria quakes struck over several weeks, and they killed tens of thousands and led to some of the first scientific studies of earthquakes.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Messina, Italy: The Messina quake and tsunami killed tens of thousands in Sicily and Calabria, and it is one of Europe's deadliest earthquakes.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Avezzano, Italy: Avezzano's quake destroyed the town in minutes, and it killed some 30,000 people in central Italy.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Skopje, North Macedonia: Skopje's quake destroyed most of the city, and international aid poured in, including from both sides of the Cold War.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Friuli, Italy: The Friuli earthquake shook northeast Italy, and the region's careful reconstruction became a model of rebuilding.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Irpinia, Italy: The Irpinia earthquake killed nearly 3,000 people in southern Italy, and criticism of the slow response led to Italy's civil protection system.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.L'Aquila, Italy: The L'Aquila quake killed over 300 people, and scientists were controversially prosecuted for their risk communication, then later acquitted.
Europe's earthquakes, in order.Amatrice, Italy: The Amatrice quake destroyed the town famous for its spaghetti all'amatriciana, and many fundraisers took inspiration from the dish.

Ancient sites, from north to south.Skara Brae, Orkney: Neolithic houses here, uncovered by a storm in 1850, contain stone dressers and beds, preserved in remarkable detail for about 5,000 years.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Hadrian's Wall: It marked the Roman Empire's northwest frontier, stretching about 118 km, dotted with forts and small gateways called milecastles.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Stonehenge: Its stones were raised in stages from about 3000 BC, and the central axis lines up with the midsummer sunrise.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Colosseum: The Colosseum opened in AD 80 with games lasting 100 days, and its cellar held animals and machinery under the arena floor.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Knossos: This Minoan palace on Crete was excavated by Arthur Evans, who linked its maze of rooms to the Minotaur's labyrinth.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Babylon: Home of the legendary Hanging Gardens, the city was ruled by Nebuchadnezzar II; its ruins lie in Iraq, south of Baghdad.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Pyramids of Giza: Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, the Great Pyramid is the only one still standing.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Abu Simbel: Ramesses II's temples were cut into blocks and moved in the 1960s to save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Aksum: Capital of an Ethiopian empire, it is famous for tall carved stelae; one was returned from Italy in 2005.
Ancient sites, from north to south.Great Zimbabwe: Its huge dry-stone walls were built without mortar, and the modern country of Zimbabwe took its name from the site.

Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Moscow: The US led a boycott that kept about 65 countries away, and Misha the bear mascot famously cried at the closing.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Calgary: A Jamaican bobsled team debuted here, inspiring the film Cool Runnings.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Barcelona: It was the Games of the original Dream Team, when American NBA stars played in the Olympics.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Nagano: It was the first Winter Games where NHL players took part, in the men's ice hockey tournament.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Turin: Shaun White won his first Olympic gold here, in the snowboard halfpipe.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Vancouver: Canada won a record 14 gold medals, then the most by any nation at a single Winter Games.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Sochi: Its estimated cost, a record for an Olympics, and a doping scandal marked these Games.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.PyeongChang: North and South Korea marched under one flag, and fielded a joint women's ice hockey team.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Beijing Winter Games: It became the first city to host both Summer and Winter Games.
Olympic Games, Summer and Winter, since.Milan Cortina: The Games are spread across northern Italian cities and Alpine venues, and Cortina had also hosted in 1956.

Carmakers, by founding year.Škoda (Laurin & Klement): Václav Laurin and Václav Klement began with bicycles in Bohemia, and the company only took the Škoda name after merging in 1925.
Carmakers, by founding year.Renault: Brothers Louis, Marcel and Fernand founded it, building on Louis's direct-drive gearbox, which he invented at age 21.
Carmakers, by founding year.Ford: Henry Ford did not invent the car, but his 1913 moving assembly line cut Model T build time from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
Carmakers, by founding year.Rolls-Royce: Charles Rolls and Henry Royce joined forces in 1904, and the Spirit of Ecstasy hood ornament first appeared in 1911.
Carmakers, by founding year.Alfa Romeo: It started as A.L.F.A. in Milan and added Nicola Romeo's name in 1920; its badge pairs Milan's red cross with a serpent.
Carmakers, by founding year.BMW: Bayerische Motoren Werke began by building aircraft engines, and its blue-and-white roundel uses the colours of Bavaria.
Carmakers, by founding year.Volvo: Volvo is Latin for I roll, and engineer Nils Bohlin's three-point seat belt of 1959 was a patent the company gave away.
Carmakers, by founding year.Porsche: Ferdinand Porsche's design office created the Volkswagen Beetle long before the first Porsche-badged car, the 356, arrived in 1948.
Carmakers, by founding year.Lamborghini: Tractor maker Ferruccio Lamborghini reportedly began building supercars after a dispute over a Ferrari's clutch.
Carmakers, by founding year.Tesla: Named for inventor Nikola Tesla, it was founded by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning, with Elon Musk joining as an investor in 2004.

Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Crocodile: Cipactli was an earth monster, and the gods tore its body apart to create the land, in Aztec myth.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.House: Calli is one of the four year-bearers, signs that could name an entire year in the 52-year cycle.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Serpent: Coatl is the root of Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent god, and of Coatlicue, mother of the gods.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Deer: The Nahuatl word mazatl, deer, also gives its name to Mazatlan, which means place of deer.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Water: Atl, water, hides in the word atlatl, the spear-thrower, and Tenochtitlan itself stood on an island in a lake.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Monkey: Ozomatli, the monkey, was linked with fun and the arts, and it is also the name of a well-known Los Angeles band.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Reed: Acatl, reed, is also a year-bearer; Cortes arrived in 1519, the year 1 Reed, which fitted the return prophecy of Quetzalcoatl.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Jaguar: Ocelotl, the jaguar, was tied to warriors, and the elite Jaguar knights were among Aztec military orders.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Movement: Ollin means movement or earthquake, and it sits at the centre of the famous Aztec Sun Stone.
Day signs of the Aztec sacred calendar.Flower: Xochitl is the sign of Xochipilli, the Flower Prince, god of art, love and games.

When these medical institutions were fou.Hôtel-Dieu de Paris: Hôtel-Dieu is often regarded as the oldest hospital in Paris, founded by a bishop, and it still operates beside Notre-Dame.
When these medical institutions were fou.St Bartholomew's, London: St Bartholomew's, 'Barts', was founded by a courtier turned monk, and it is the oldest hospital in Britain still on its original site.
When these medical institutions were fou.Bethlem (Bedlam): Bethlem began as a priory and later became a psychiatric hospital whose nickname 'Bedlam' became a word for chaos.
When these medical institutions were fou.Charité, Berlin: The Charité began as a plague house, and it later became a leading medical school where Robert Koch and Rudolf Virchow worked.
When these medical institutions were fou.Massachusetts General: Massachusetts General in Boston is where ether anesthesia was first publicly shown in 1846, in what is now called the Ether Dome.
When these medical institutions were fou.Great Ormond Street: Great Ormond Street was Britain's first hospital for children, and J.M. Barrie gave the rights to Peter Pan to it.
When these medical institutions were fou.Johns Hopkins Hospital: Johns Hopkins Hospital opened with a tradition of combining care, teaching and research, which shaped modern American medicine.
When these medical institutions were fou.CDC: The CDC began as an office to fight malaria in the American South, and it is now based in Atlanta.
When these medical institutions were fou.NHS: The NHS was founded on the principle of care free at the point of use, and its first patient reportedly was 13-year-old Sylvia Diggory.
When these medical institutions were fou.Doctors Without Borders: Doctors Without Borders, founded in France by a group of doctors and journalists, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999.

How long is the pregnancy?.Virginia opossum: The Virginia opossum is the only marsupial north of Mexico, and its babies are born tiny, about the size of a honeybee, and crawl to the pouch.
How long is the pregnancy?.House mouse: A female mouse can have litters about monthly, with up to ten pups each, which is why mice populations can explode quickly.
How long is the pregnancy?.Rabbit: Rabbits can become pregnant again almost immediately after giving birth, which helped make them a symbol of fertility.
How long is the pregnancy?.Dog: Puppies are born blind and deaf, with eyes opening after about two weeks, and the mother keeps them warm in a den-like spot.
How long is the pregnancy?.Pig: A traditional farmers' rule says three months, three weeks and three days, which comes to about 114 days.
How long is the pregnancy?.Sheep: Ewes often have twins, and lambs can stand and nurse within minutes of birth, a trait that helps them keep up with the flock.
How long is the pregnancy?.Human: Counted from the last period, it is about 40 weeks, and the due date is calculated by Naegele's rule, which adds 280 days.
How long is the pregnancy?.Horse: A foal can stand within about an hour of birth and run with the herd soon after, which is an adaptation to avoid predators.
How long is the pregnancy?.Giraffe: The calf falls about 1.8 m to the ground at birth, since the mother gives birth standing up, and then stands within an hour or so.
How long is the pregnancy?.African elephant: It is the longest of any land mammal, and the calf weighs about 100 kg at birth and is looked after by many aunts in the herd.

American football by the numbers.Points for a safety: A safety happens when the offense is tackled in its own end zone, and the defending team also gets the ball back by free kick.
American football by the numbers.Points for a field goal: The longest in NFL history is 66 yards, kicked by Justin Tucker in 2021 as time expired.
American football by the numbers.Downs to gain 10 yards: Offenses get four downs to move ten yards, a rule set in 1912; before that, teams had only three.
American football by the numbers.Points for a touchdown: A touchdown has been worth six points only since 1912; in the 1880s it was worth just two.
American football by the numbers.Yards for a first down: Close calls on first downs are settled by a 10-yard chain carried out onto the field by the sideline crew.
American football by the numbers.Players per side: Each team fields eleven, but an NFL roster holds 53 players, with specialists for kicking, snapping and special teams.
American football by the numbers.Ball weight (oz): The nickname pigskin comes from early balls made with pig bladders; modern NFL footballs are made from cowhide.
American football by the numbers.NFL goalpost width (ft): NFL goalposts are 18 feet 6 inches apart, while high school posts are wider, at 23 feet 4 inches.
American football by the numbers.Field width (yd): Fifty-three and a third yards is exactly 160 feet, a neat figure in feet for a field measured in yards.
American football by the numbers.Goal line to goal line (yd): With a 10-yard end zone at each end, the full playing field including both end zones runs 120 yards.

When these hoaxes fooled the world.Psalmanazar's fake Formosa: A Frenchman posing as a native of Formosa, he invented a language and alphabet before confessing.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.Mary Toft's rabbit births: She claimed to give birth to rabbits, and surgeons were fooled until she confessed.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.Cardiff Giant: Carved from gypsum, it was buried on a farm in New York and 'discovered'; P. T. Barnum made a copy.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.Piltdown Man: This fake skull paired a human cranium with an orangutan jaw, fooled scientists for decades and was exposed in 1953.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.Cottingley Fairies: Two girls took photos with paper cut-out fairies, and Arthur Conan Doyle endorsed them.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.Loch Ness 'Surgeon's Photo': A toy submarine fitted with a sculpted head made the famous Loch Ness photo, and a confession came in 1994.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.BBC spaghetti harvest: The BBC's April Fools' report about spaghetti growing on trees led viewers to ask how to grow their own.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.Hitler Diaries: Stern magazine paid millions for forged diaries made by Konrad Kujau, which were exposed within weeks.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.'Alien Autopsy' film: Ray Santilli's black-and-white film turned out in 2006 to be an admitted re-creation.
When these hoaxes fooled the world.Balloon Boy: Falcon Heene's father claimed the boy had floated away in a balloon, but the boy had been hiding in the attic.

First ascents of famous peaks.Mont Blanc: Mont Blanc was first climbed by Jacques Balmat and Michel Paccard, an event often marked as the birth of mountaineering.
First ascents of famous peaks.Matterhorn: Edward Whymper reached the top, but four of the seven in his party died on the descent when a rope snapped.
First ascents of famous peaks.Kilimanjaro: Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller reached the summit of Africa's highest mountain.
First ascents of famous peaks.Aconcagua: Swiss climber Matthias Zurbriggen reached the summit alone, the highest peak outside Asia.
First ascents of famous peaks.Denali: Hudson Stuck's party climbed it. Once called Mount McKinley, it was officially renamed in 2015.
First ascents of famous peaks.Eiger north face: Its northern wall is nicknamed the Murder Wall, and Heckmair's team of four first climbed it.
First ascents of famous peaks.Annapurna: Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal made the first ascent of any 8,000-meter peak.
First ascents of famous peaks.Everest: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the top, and the news reached London on Coronation day.
First ascents of famous peaks.K2: Italians Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli summited the Savage Mountain, one of the deadliest peaks.
First ascents of famous peaks.Vinson Massif: The highest mountain in Antarctica was first climbed by an American expedition.

Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Chamomile tea: Technically an herbal infusion, not tea, since it isn't made from the tea plant, it contains no caffeine.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Decaf coffee (8 oz): Decaf isn't caffeine-free; the process removes about 97 percent of it.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Milk chocolate bar (1.55 oz): The chocolate also carries theobromine, a milder stimulant that is toxic to dogs.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Coca-Cola (12 oz can): The name came from coca leaf and kola nut, and early recipes contained cocaine until about 1903.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Black tea (8 oz): Black, green, white and oolong teas all come from the same plant; the difference lies in how much the leaves are oxidized.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Single espresso shot: A shot has less caffeine than a cup of brewed coffee, as it is a small volume, though much more concentrated.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Red Bull (8.4 oz can): It was based on the Thai drink Krating Daeng, whose name means red gaur, which Dietrich Mateschitz discovered on a trip.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Brewed coffee (8 oz): Coffee beans are the seeds of a cherry-like fruit, and legend credits an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi with discovering them.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.Monster Energy (16 oz): It launched in 2002 from Hansen Natural, which was later renamed Monster Beverage, and became a rival to Red Bull.
Caffeine in a typical serving of each.5-hour Energy shot: Launched in 2004 in a tiny bottle, a shot delivers about as much caffeine as two cups of coffee.

Milestones beneath the waves.Turtle, first combat sub: David Bushnell's one-man, hand-cranked egg-shaped submarine tried to attach a bomb to HMS Eagle in New York Harbor and failed.
Milestones beneath the waves.Fulton's Nautilus: Robert Fulton built it for Napoleon's France; navies weren't convinced, and he turned to steamboats.
Milestones beneath the waves.H.L. Hunley sinks a warship: It was the first submarine to sink an enemy warship, the USS Housatonic, then vanished with its crew and was raised in 2000.
Milestones beneath the waves.USS Holland commissioned: John Holland designed it; it ran on a gasoline engine on the surface and electric motors underwater.
Milestones beneath the waves.Nuclear USS Nautilus launched: The first nuclear-powered ship reached the North Pole beneath the ice in 1958.
Milestones beneath the waves.Trieste dives Challenger Deep: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached about 10,900 meters, the deepest point in the ocean.
Milestones beneath the waves.Alvin commissioned: The Woods Hole submersible found hydrothermal vents in 1977 and explored the Titanic in 1986.
Milestones beneath the waves.USS Ohio commissioned: The lead boat of the Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines, among the largest in the US fleet, later converted to carry cruise missiles.
Milestones beneath the waves.Cameron's Deepsea Challenger: James Cameron's solo dive to the Challenger Deep in 2012 took the sub down vertically, like a torpedo, in about two and a half hours.
Milestones beneath the waves.Five Deeps Expedition ends: Victor Vescovo dived to the deepest point of all five oceans, in the submersible Limiting Factor.

Finnish numbers, by the value they name.yksi: Finnish belongs to the Uralic family, closer to Estonian and Hungarian than to its Scandinavian or Russian neighbors.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.kaksi: Finnish nouns have around 15 cases, so even a number changes shape with its job in a sentence.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.kolme: Finnish has no grammatical gender and one pronoun, hän, covers both 'he' and 'she'.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.neljä: The ä is a distinct vowel, and in Finnish the length of vowels and consonants can change a word's meaning.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.viisi: Finnish is spelled almost exactly as it sounds, and the stress always lands on the first syllable.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.kuusi: This word also means 'spruce', so the same word names both a number and a tree; context does the sorting.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.seitsemän: Seitsemän veljestä, 'Seven Brothers' by Aleksis Kivi in 1870, is considered the first major novel in Finnish.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.kahdeksan: Eight and nine are traditionally explained as 'two short of ten' and 'one short of ten', hiding a trace of kaksi inside.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.yhdeksän: Nine is traditionally read as 'one short of ten', which is why yksi seems to lurk inside the word.
Finnish numbers, by the value they name.kymmenen: Ten is round, but so is the sauna count: Finland has roughly three million saunas for about 5.5 million people.

From pool to planet: how long is it?.Olympic swimming pool: The standard length is why it's called long course; short course pools are 25 meters.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.Soccer pitch: FIFA gives a range of lengths, and 105 by 68 meters is the common recommended size.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.Central Park (end to end): About 4 km long, this man-made park was designed by Olmsted and Vaux and built in the mid-1800s.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.The Las Vegas Strip: Most of its famous casinos are actually outside Las Vegas city limits, in Paradise, Nevada.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.A marathon: The 42.195 km distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics so it could start at Windsor Castle.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.The Channel Tunnel: About 38 km lie under the sea, the longest undersea section of any tunnel in the world.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.The Panama Canal: It opened in 1914, and ships are lifted about 26 meters by locks up to Gatun Lake.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.Route 66: Nicknamed the Mother Road, it ran from Chicago to Santa Monica and was decommissioned in 1985.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.Great Wall (all sections): It's not one wall but many built over centuries, and the myth that it's visible from space is false.
From pool to planet: how long is it?.Earth's equator: Earth bulges at the equator, and the planet spins there at about 1,670 km/h.

Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.Classic Instagram post: Instagram's original square format let anyone crop a photo into a square, a nod to Polaroid and old medium-format cameras. It dropped the rule in 2015.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.Old 1280x1024 office monitor: Old 17-inch office LCD monitors often used this squarish 5:4 shape, which gave more vertical room for documents and spreadsheets.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.Classic CRT TV: Television used 4:3 for most of the 20th century, a ratio inherited from early cinema's Academy format of 1932.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.35mm photo: The shape of a classic 35mm film frame, 36 by 24 mm, which is why many prints are 6x4 inches.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.MacBook screen (pre-2021): Apple's laptops and many monitors used this shape for years, giving room for toolbars while still looking widescreen. MacBook Pros added a camera notch in 2021.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.HDTV: The standard for HD and 4K television and most computer screens. It was a compromise chosen in the 1980s between 4:3 and cinema's wide shapes.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.LG G6 phone: Phones of 2017 started to use the taller 18:9 shape, also called 2:1, which puts more screen in a narrow device, LG's G6 among the first.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.iPhone X screen: Apple's 2017 iPhone X reached this tall shape with a notch at the top that held the sensors for Face ID.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.Ultrawide monitor: This cinematic 21:9 shape is close to the wide format of many films, and monitors using it can show two windows side by side.
Screen shapes, from squarest to widest.Super ultrawide monitor: Equal to two 16:9 screens side by side, this 32:9 shape is popular with gamers and traders who want a single huge display.

Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Cotton: Cotton for the second year is a modest gift, given when a marriage is still young.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Leather: Leather is the traditional third-year gift, praised for being durable.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Bronze: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, and its discovery gave the Bronze Age its name.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Steel: Steel is an alloy of iron and a little carbon, strong and long-lasting.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Silk: Silk was first made in China, and the secret was kept for thousands of years.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Lace: It's a delicate material, handmade for centuries on bobbins or with needles.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Ivory: Ivory is an awkward choice today, as the ivory trade is widely banned and many prefer substitutes.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Coral: Coral is actually colonies of tiny animals; red coral was long prized for jewellery.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Sapphire: It's the same mineral as ruby; sapphire is the name for every colour except red.
Lesser-known wedding anniversary gifts.Emerald: Emerald is a form of beryl, like aquamarine; its green comes from traces of chromium or vanadium.

Tech companies older than you think.Siemens: The company began as a telegraph workshop in Berlin, and it now builds everything from trains to medical scanners.
Tech companies older than you think.Nokia: It started as a pulp mill in Finland, and it got its name from a town and river, and it produced rubber boots before phones.
Tech companies older than you think.Ericsson: Founded by Lars Magnus Ericsson in Stockholm, it began by repairing telegraph equipment, and today it builds cellular networks.
Tech companies older than you think.Nintendo: It started by making handmade playing cards in Kyoto, and its name is often said to mean 'leave luck to heaven'.
Tech companies older than you think.Philips: The Dutch company began by making light bulbs in Eindhoven, and it later co-invented the compact disc with Sony.
Tech companies older than you think.Xerox (as Haloid): The firm that eventually invented the photocopier was a small photographic paper maker in Rochester, New York, before it was renamed.
Tech companies older than you think.Panasonic: The Japanese electronics maker was founded by Konosuke Matsushita, who began with a modified light socket.
Tech companies older than you think.Canon: It began as the Precision Optical Instruments Laboratory, and its name came from the Buddhist goddess Kannon.
Tech companies older than you think.Samsung: It began as a trading firm in Daegu, and its name means 'three stars', and it exported dried fish and noodles.
Tech companies older than you think.Sony: It started as a small Tokyo repair shop with just 20 employees, and it created the first Walkman in 1979.

Things athletes throw or slide.Olympic archery arrow: Olympic recurve archers shoot from 70 meters at a target face where the gold center is just 12.2 cm wide, like hitting a coin from afar.
Things athletes throw or slide.Steel-tip dart: Darts must weigh no more than 50 g; the highest possible score with three darts is 180, three treble 20s, and the best players hit it often.
Things athletes throw or slide.Ice hockey puck: Pucks are frozen before games so they bounce less on the ice, and a slapshot from a top player can travel well over 150 km/h.
Things athletes throw or slide.Women's javelin: The javelin's design was changed in 1986, moving its center of gravity forward, after Uwe Hohn threw 104.80 m and threatened spectators.
Things athletes throw or slide.Men's javelin: Jan Železný, a three-time Olympic champion, threw 98.48 m in 1996, a men's javelin world record that has stood ever since.
Things athletes throw or slide.Women's discus: Gabriele Reinsch of East Germany set the women's discus world record, 76.80 m, in 1988, and no one has come close in decades.
Things athletes throw or slide.Men's discus: Throwers spin about one and a half turns to hurl it, a pose captured in the ancient Greek statue Discobolus by Myron.
Things athletes throw or slide.Women's shot: Natalya Lisovskaya's 22.63 m throw from 1987 is still the women's shot put world record, the target for every thrower since.
Things athletes throw or slide.Men's shot: The shot is pushed, not thrown: it must stay close to the neck until release. The men's shot weighs 16 pounds, hence the odd 7.26 kg.
Things athletes throw or slide.Curling stone: Curling stones are made of granite from Ailsa Craig, a Scottish island, prized for dense rock that rarely cracks and absorbs little water.

Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Moon: Dante put those who broke their vows in the sphere of the Moon, which is the dimmest, and Piccarda Donati appears there.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Mercury: Mercury houses spirits who did good to earn fame; the Emperor Justinian speaks there, summing up Roman history in a long speech.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Venus: Venus holds the spirits who loved, including Charles Martel; Dante named it after the Roman goddess of love.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Sun: The Sun holds the wise, including Thomas Aquinas and Bonaventure, whose spirits circle Dante like a glowing garland.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Mars: In Mars warriors of the faith form a cross of light, and Dante meets his ancestor Cacciaguida, who foretells his exile from Florence.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Jupiter: In Jupiter just rulers form a giant eagle out of light, which speaks to Dante as a single voice made of many souls.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Saturn: Saturn is the realm of contemplatives, reached by a golden ladder reaching beyond sight; Peter Damian and Benedict are among those there.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Fixed Stars: In the sphere of Fixed Stars, Dante is examined by Saints Peter, James and John on faith, hope and love.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Primum Mobile: The name means first moved; it spins fastest and drives all inner spheres, and here Dante learns the order of the angels.
Heavens of Dante's Paradiso, from Earth.Empyrean: Beyond space and time, the Empyrean holds the Celestial Rose, where Dante finally glimpses God, guided by Bernard of Clairvaux.

Trailblazing moments in women's sport.First female Olympic champion: Charlotte Cooper won the tennis singles at Paris 1900, the first Games to admit women.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Ederle swims the Channel: She crossed the English Channel in under 15 hours, beating the men's record by about two hours.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Babe Didrikson's Olympic golds: At the 1932 Los Angeles Games she won gold in javelin and hurdles and silver in high jump, and later became a pro golfer.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Althea Gibson wins Wimbledon: She was the first Black champion at Wimbledon, and won the US Championships the same year.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Switzer runs Boston: She ran Boston as 'K.V. Switzer', and an official tried to physically pull her from the course.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Title IX passes: The US law banned sex discrimination in federally funded education, hugely increasing girls' and women's sports participation.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Battle of the Sexes: Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs in straight sets before about 90 million television viewers.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.First women's Olympic marathon: Joan Benoit won in Los Angeles, and Gabriele Andersen-Schiess's staggering finish in the heat became an enduring image.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Women's Olympic boxing: Women's boxing debuted at London 2012 with three weight classes, and Britain's Nicola Adams won the first flyweight gold.
Trailblazing moments in women's sport.Women's Olympic ski jumping: After a long legal fight, women's ski jumping joined at Sochi 2014, with Germany's Carina Vogt taking the first gold.

Home appliances, oldest to newest.Lawn mower: Mowers date from Edwin Budding, a British engineer, who got the idea from a machine used to trim cloth at a textile mill.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Sewing machine (Howe): Elias Howe's patent triggered the 'sewing machine wars', a long legal battle with Isaac Singer and others over rights to the design.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Electric fan: The first electric fans were made by Schuyler Wheeler, and they were status items before air conditioning.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Powered vacuum cleaner: Hubert Cecil Booth's early vacuum cleaner was so large it was pulled by a horse and parked outside buildings while hoses reached through windows.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Air conditioner (Carrier): Willis Carrier's invention aimed to control humidity for a printing plant, not to cool people, and it later changed where people could live.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Electric washing machine: Alva Fisher's Thor washing machine was an early electric model, and it freed many households from laborious hand scrubbing.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Pop-up toaster: Charles Strite invented the pop-up toaster for factory workers tired of burnt toast, and its mass popularity grew after Wonder Bread sold sliced loaves.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near a radar tube and invented the microwave oven in the process.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Dyson bagless vacuum: James Dyson built over 5,000 prototypes before his cyclone vacuum, and it eliminated the need for bags.
Home appliances, oldest to newest.Roomba robot vacuum: iRobot's first Roomba cleaned floors on its own, and the company previously made robots for military and space use.

European rivers by length.Thames: The longest river entirely in England, though only about 346 km, and it ran through the heart of an empire.
European rivers by length.Tiber: Legend says the twins Romulus and Remus were found on its banks, before Rome's founding.
European rivers by length.Seine: Its banks hosted the opening ceremony of the 2024 Olympics, with athletes sailing by boat through Paris.
European rivers by length.Loire: The longest river in France, its valley is a UNESCO site known for its many Renaissance chateaux.
European rivers by length.Elbe: It rises in the Czech mountains and runs past Dresden and Hamburg before reaching the North Sea.
European rivers by length.Rhine: A rocky cliff on its banks gave rise to the Lorelei legend, in which a siren lured sailors to doom.
European rivers by length.Don: Russia's river of the Cossacks, immortalised in Sholokhov's novel 'And Quiet Flows the Don'.
European rivers by length.Dnieper: It flows through Russia, Belarus and Ukraine, passing through Kyiv before reaching the Black Sea.
European rivers by length.Danube: It flows through or along the borders of ten countries, more than any other river in the world.
European rivers by length.Volga: Russians call it 'Mother Volga'; it is the longest river in Europe and drains into the Caspian Sea.

Nature's giants by area.Central Park: Opened in the 1850s, this Manhattan park was designed by Olmsted and Vaux, and nearly everything in it, including the lakes and hills, is man-made.
Nature's giants by area.Dead Sea: Its shores are the lowest dry land on Earth, over 400 metres below sea level. The water is so salty that swimmers float easily.
Nature's giants by area.Grand Canyon National Park: One of America's first national parks, it draws several million visitors a year. The canyon within it is up to 29 km wide in places.
Nature's giants by area.Yellowstone: Established in 1872, it is widely held to be the world's first national park. It sits atop a huge volcanic hot spot with thousands of geysers and hot springs.
Nature's giants by area.Serengeti National Park: Every year more than a million wildebeest and hundreds of thousands of zebras migrate across it in search of fresh grass in a huge circuit.
Nature's giants by area.Lake Victoria: Africa's largest lake is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. It is the main source of the White Nile, the longer branch of the Nile.
Nature's giants by area.Great Barrier Reef: This reef system is made of nearly 3,000 individual reefs and around 900 islands, and it can be seen from outer space.
Nature's giants by area.Caspian Sea: Despite its name, it is the largest inland body of water on Earth, a lake, shared by five countries. Its water is salty, though less than the ocean.
Nature's giants by area.Greenland ice sheet: If it melted completely, global sea levels would rise by about seven metres. It holds the second-largest body of ice on Earth, after Antarctica.
Nature's giants by area.Amazon rainforest: The world's largest tropical rainforest holds about one in ten of all known species. It spans nine countries, with most of it in Brazil.

Taking a plane trip, in order.Check in and drop bags: Checked bags get three-letter airport codes, like LHR for London Heathrow, so ground crews can route them to the right plane.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Security screening: Airport liquid limits of 100 ml came in during 2006, after UK police foiled a plot to blow up transatlantic flights with liquid explosives.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Wait at the gate: Airlines sometimes oversell flights, betting that a few ticketed passengers won't show, which is why gate agents may offer rewards for volunteers.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Board the plane: Studies of boarding find that letting window seats on first is quicker than the usual back-to-front order.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Taxi to the runway: Jets taxi slowly, usually under about 30 miles an hour, and pilots steer on the ground with a small tiller or the rudder pedals.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Takeoff: Airliners lift off at roughly 250 kilometres an hour, and a heavy fully loaded jet may use more than two kilometres of runway.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Climb to cruising altitude: Cruising altitude is typically around 10,000 metres, where the air is too thin to breathe, so cabins are pressurised.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Begin the descent: Airliners can descend with engines at idle, gliding over a long distance, which saves fuel.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Touchdown: Planes slow after touchdown using brakes, spoilers and reverse thrust, which redirects engine power forward to help stop the jet.
Taking a plane trip, in order.Baggage claim: Only a few bags per thousand passengers are mishandled, so the chance your bag is lost is small, and most are found.

Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.Wynne's first crossword: Liverpool-born Arthur Wynne's diamond-shaped word-cross appeared in the New York World; a later typo flipped it to cross-word.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.First crossword book: Simon and Schuster's first crossword book came with a pencil attached, and its huge success set off a nationwide craze.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.The Times crossword: Britain's cryptic crosswords rely on wordplay in the clues, and the Times puzzle became a national institution.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.NYT crossword: The paper had long resisted puzzles, but the first one ran in February 1942, edited by Margaret Farrar.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.Will Shortz becomes editor: Shortz is believed to be the only person with a college degree in enigmatology, which he designed himself at Indiana University.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.Clinton-Dole puzzle: An Election Day puzzle had a clue whose answer could be either candidate's name, and the crossing words worked for both.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.Wordplay documentary: The film follows Will Shortz and puzzle fans, including Jon Stewart and Bill Clinton, at the American Crossword Puzzle Tournament.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.NYT Mini: A tiny crossword that can be solved in a minute, it drew many people into the Times games app.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.NYT Spelling Bee: Players make words from seven letters, always using the centre one; finding a pangram that uses all seven is the real thrill.
Crossword and word-puzzle milestones.Wordle launches: Josh Wardle made it for his partner, who loved word games; the New York Times bought it in early 2022 for a reported price in the low seven figures.
